paper.title: Interethnic Union Formation Among 1.5- and Second-Generation Immigrants: The Role of Cultural Proximity
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is given. The paper states (p. …

registers.name_in_paper: different administrative registers maintained by Statistics Denmark
registers.role: outcomes (registered marriages and cohabiting unions), sample frame, individual controls, and the population counts used to build province-level opportunity structures
linkage: supplies the unique personal identification number that allows registers to be merged

linkages: All residents of Denmark hold a unique personal identification number (Danish Civil Registration System), which lets information from different Statistics Denmark administrative registers be merged.

Individuals are linked to partners through registered marriages and through shared address (the cohabitation proxy: same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes less than 15 years apart in age sharing an address without kinship).
Individuals are linked to their parents' country of birth and citizenship to assign generational status and country of origin.

Individuals are linked to their province of residence (11 NUTS-3 provinces) and to annual province-by-origin-group population counts to build relative group size, within-group sex ratio and within-group educational similarity.

National origin groups are linked to external country-level sources: dominant religion (Pew Research Center 2015), value indexes (Inglehart–Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022, WVS 2022) and language/writing-system classification.

sample.universe: 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups. 1.5-generation immigrants were born 1966–1986, were aged 0–17 on arrival in Denmark and resided in Denmark at age 18. Second-generation immigrants were born in Denmark 1966–1986 to immigrant parents, neither of whom was a Danish citizen or born in Denmark.
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (person–period format), from age 18 until first union formation or right censoring
selection_rules: Restrict to 1.5- and second-generation immigrants as defined above (birth cohorts 1966–1986).
1.5-generation immigrants must have arrived aged 0–17 and have resided in Denmark at age 18.
Enter the risk set on turning 18 only if not already in a union.
Follow until the first union formation; only first unions are considered, not second or higher-order unions.
Right censor at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period (2016).

Country mergers and splits are coded into coherent units retained throughout (former Soviet Union merged with Russia; former Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro merged into 'Serbia Montenegro' with Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia kept separate; Czechoslovakia merged with the Czech Republic; East and West Germany kept together as Germany).
Separate estimation samples for men (316,792 person-years) and women (219,086 person-years).
In the descriptive Table 2, countries with fewer than 100 individuals are not shown and cells deriving from fewer than 5 individuals are suppressed.
sample.n_observations: 535,878 person-years (316,792 for men and 219,086 for women in the Table 4 models)

construction_notes: A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union. Cohabiting unions are defined as two persons living at the same address with a common child, or as two people of different sexes whose age difference is less than 15 years who share the same address without being related by kinship; the authors note this proxy may misclassify roommates.

Three competing event types: (1) interethnic union with a native (partner and partner's parents born in Denmark), (2) interethnic union with an immigrant from another country of origin, (3) intraethnic union with a same-country immigrant.

Religion is the dominant religion of the country of origin (Pew Research Center 2015), coded Protestant / Catholic / other Christian / Muslim / Hindu, Buddhist or other; the reference category in Table 4 is Protestant.

Values are the absolute difference between the country of origin's and Denmark's scores on the two Inglehart–Welzel indexes (traditional vs secular–rational; survival vs self-expression), from the Inglehart–Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022 (WVS data 2005–2022). Scales run from −2 to +2, with a few countries including Denmark reaching +3 on the survival vs self-expression dimension. For about 25 percent of countries the index is extrapolated from a neighbouring country.

Language groups the country of origin by primary spoken language and writing system: Scandinavian (reference), the core Anglosphere, other English-speaking plus Latin/Cyrillic/Greek alphabet countries, and other countries.
Relative group size = number of first- or second-generation immigrants of the person's national origin per thousand of the province population aged 18–40.
Within-group sex ratio = (proportion of men aged 18–40 / proportion of women aged 18–40) in the national origin group in the province, × 100.

Within-group educational similarity = percentage of all opposite-sex members aged 25–40 of the national origin group in the province with the same educational level as the individual, using three educational levels; the lower age limit is 25 rather than 18 to avoid bias from people still enrolled.
Opportunity-structure variables are measured on 1 January of year t and related to unions formed during the following year.

Local partner markets are the 11 Danish NUTS-3 provinces (North Jutland, East Jutland, West Jutland, South Jutland, Funen, Bornholm, West and South Zealand, East Zealand, North Zealand, Copenhagen City, Copenhagen Surroundings).

Individual controls: first year of observation (year of turning 18), generational status (second generation; 1.5 generation arriving aged 0–5, 6–11, 12–16; unknown, about 1 percent), and time-varying educational attainment in six levels plus a missing category (education missing for about 20 percent of the analysis sample).
Except for the categorical variables, all variables in Table 4 are standardized so coefficient sizes can be compared.
Three-level models for local partner markets were not used because there are only 11 provinces, too few for reasonable variance estimates.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Catholic' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, relative to Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Catholic (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

estimand.target_population: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 316792 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for Catholic (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
The running text does not discuss this particular cell of Table 4; the sign and significance are read from the table.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 8875 union formations of this type for men; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 316792 person-years of exposure for men. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 8875/316792 = 0.028015. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

value.as_printed: log( p(r)tig / (1 - p(r)tig) ) = α(r)0 + α(r)1 t + α(r)1 t2 + β(r)′xtig + γ(r)′cg + θ(r)′otigp + s(r)yt + v(r)p + u(r)g + ε(r)tig , r = 1, 2, 3
value.lhs: log( p(r)tig / (1 − p(r)tig) ) — the log odds of the event-specific discrete-time hazard of event type r, defined as p(r)tig = Pr(ytig = r | yt−1,ig = 0)

terms.parameter: α(r)1 (printed; apparently a typo for α(r)2)
u(r)g (random intercept across national origin groups)

prior_findings_compared.citation: Alba and Foner 2015; Dribe and Lundh 2011; Kalmijn and van Tubergen 2006, 2010; Wachter 2022
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Our ﬁndings supplement earlier studies from Western Europe, which have found that ﬁrst- and second-generation immigrants from Muslim countries are less likely to form interethnic unions with natives and more likely to form intraethnic unions with same-country immigrants

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Odds ratios for the time-varying individual-level factors (time, time squared, generational status, educational level) are examined but reported only in Table A1 of the online supplementary material, not in Table 4.

anchor_quote.text: We also see modest differences in union formation patterns across different types of Christians.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Catholic' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first intraethnic union with a same-country immigrant, relative to Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Catholic (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from the same country of origin as the respondent. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Other Christian' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, relative to Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Other Christian (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from a different country of origin than the respondent's own. ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
Table 4 labels this category 'Other Christian'; the running text on p. 487 refers to the same group as 'Orthodox Christian' countries.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
The running text does not discuss this particular cell of Table 4; the sign and significance are read from the table.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 3707 union formations of this type for men; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 316792 person-years of exposure for men. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 3707/316792 = 0.011702. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for Muslim (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 12667 union formations of this type for men; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 316792 person-years of exposure for men. claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Muslim' is associated with lower odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native than coming from Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Muslim (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

magnitude.interpretation: the odds of interethnic union formation with natives are approximately one-third of those for their counterparts from Protestant countries

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Odds ratios for the time-varying individual-level factors (time, time squared, generational status, educational level) are examined but reported only in Table A1 of the online supplementary material, not in Table 4.

anchor_quote.text: For female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants from Muslim countries, the odds of interethnic union formation with natives are approximately one-third of those for their counterparts from Protestant countries.

claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Muslim' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with an immigrant from another country of origin, relative to Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Muslim (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from a different country of origin than the respondent's own. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for Muslim (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
The running text does not discuss this particular cell of Table 4; the sign and significance are read from the table.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 3724 union formations of this type for women; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 219086 person-years of exposure for women. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 3724/219086 = 0.016998. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Hindu, Buddhist, or other' is associated with higher odds of forming a first intraethnic union with a same-country immigrant than coming from Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Hindu, Buddhist, or other' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with an immigrant from another country of origin, relative to Protestant-majority countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Hindu, Buddhist, or other (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant)

definition.value: The dominant religion of the individual's country of origin, taken from Pew Research Center data; countries of origin are coded into five groups (Protestant; Catholic; other Christian; Muslim; Hindu, Buddhist, or other religions). The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Protestant-majority countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from a different country of origin than the respondent's own. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for Hindu, Buddhist, or other (dominant religion of country of origin; ref. = Protestant) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed for the individual over the whole observation period (ages 18-40, 1986-2016).

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from the same country of origin as the respondent. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Protestant-majority

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, a one standard deviation increase in traditional values vs secular-rational values is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, net of the cultural factors, the other opportunity structures and individual controls.

treatment.label: Traditional values vs secular-rational values

definition.value: A country-level measure of value distance from Denmark: the absolute value of the difference between the country of origin's score and Denmark's score on an Inglehart-Welzel index (scales run from -2 to +2, Denmark reaching +3 on the survival vs self-expression dimension), using the scores behind the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022 (WVS 2022, data from 2005-2022). A low number means the country is culturally proximate to Denmark, a high number culturally distant. For about 25 percent of countries the index is extrapolated from a neighbouring country. The variable is standardized in the model.

timing.value: Time-invariant country-of-origin characteristic (the paper notes its value measures are time-invariant), fixed over the whole observation period.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized country-level value distance from Denmark

definition.value: A country-level measure of value distance from Denmark: the absolute value of the difference between the country of origin's score and Denmark's score on an Inglehart-Welzel index (scales run from -2 to +2, Denmark reaching +3 on the survival vs self-expression dimension), using the scores behind the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022 (WVS 2022, data from 2005-2022). definition.value: A country-level measure of value distance from Denmark: the absolute value of the difference between the country of origin's score and Denmark's score on an Inglehart-Welzel index (scales run from -2 to +2, Denmark reaching +3 on the survival vs self-expression dimension), using the scores behind the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022 (WVS 2022, data from 2005-2022). definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, a one standard deviation increase in survival values vs self-expression values is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first intraethnic union with a same-country immigrant, net of the cultural factors, the other opportunity structures and individual controls.

treatment.label: Survival values vs self-expression values

definition.value: A country-level measure of value distance from Denmark: the absolute value of the difference between the country of origin's score and Denmark's score on an Inglehart-Welzel index (scales run from -2 to +2, Denmark reaching +3 on the survival vs self-expression dimension), using the scores behind the Inglehart-Welzel Cultural Map of the World 2022 (WVS 2022, data from 2005-2022). A low number means the country is culturally proximate to Denmark, a high number culturally distant. For about 25 percent of countries the index is extrapolated from a neighbouring country. The variable is standardized in the model.

timing.value: Time-invariant country-of-origin characteristic (the paper notes its value measures are time-invariant), fixed over the whole observation period.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from the same country of origin as the respondent. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized country-level value distance from Denmark

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the standardized measure Survival values vs self-expression values is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

treatment.label: The core Anglosphere (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian)

definition.value: The language group of the individual's country of origin, based on the country's primary spoken language and primary writing system, coded into four groups: Scandinavian; the core Anglosphere; other English-speaking countries and countries using the Latin, Cyrillic or Greek alphabet; and other countries. The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Scandinavian-language countries of origin as the omitted reference.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

definition.value: The language group of the individual's country of origin, based on the country's primary spoken language and primary writing system, coded into four groups: Scandinavian; the core Anglosphere; other English-speaking countries and countries using the Latin, Cyrillic or Greek alphabet; and other countries. key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for The core Anglosphere (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 316792 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the indicator for Other English-speaking (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian) is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 12667 union formations of this type for men; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 316792 person-years of exposure for men. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 12667/316792 = 0.039985. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Other English-speaking' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, relative to Scandinavian-speaking countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Other English-speaking (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian)

definition.value: The language group of the individual's country of origin, based on the country's primary spoken language and primary writing system, coded into four groups: Scandinavian; the core Anglosphere; other English-speaking countries and countries using the Latin, Cyrillic or Greek alphabet; and other countries. The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Scandinavian-language countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed over the whole observation period.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Scandinavian-speaking

treatment.label: Other English-speaking (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian)

definition.value: The language group of the individual's country of origin, based on the country's primary spoken language and primary writing system, coded into four groups: Scandinavian; the core Anglosphere; other English-speaking countries and countries using the Latin, Cyrillic or Greek alphabet; and other countries. The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Scandinavian-language countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed over the whole observation period.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from a different country of origin than the respondent's own. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Scandinavian-speaking

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.

dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)

population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 3724 union formations of this type for women; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 219086 person-years of exposure for women. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 3724/219086 = 0.016998. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, coming from a country of origin classified as 'Other' is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, relative to Scandinavian-speaking countries of origin, net of the other cultural factors, opportunity structures in the local partner market and individual controls.

treatment.label: Other (language group of country of origin; ref. = Scandinavian)

definition.value: The language group of the individual's country of origin, based on the country's primary spoken language and primary writing system, coded into four groups: Scandinavian; the core Anglosphere; other English-speaking countries and countries using the Latin, Cyrillic or Greek alphabet; and other countries. The coefficient is an indicator for this category, with Scandinavian-language countries of origin as the omitted reference.

timing.value: Time-invariant characteristic of the country of origin, fixed over the whole observation period.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio relative to immigrants whose country of origin is Scandinavian-speaking

estimand.target_population: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18.
