population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
The paper prints no exact p-value; non-significance is inferred from the absence of an asterisk in Table 4.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 8875 union formations of this type for men; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 316792 person-years of exposure for men. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 8875/316792 = 0.028015. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.

claims.statement: Among female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, a one standard deviation increase in relative group size decreases the odds of forming a first interethnic union with an immigrant from another country of origin, net of the cultural factors, the other opportunity structures and individual controls.

treatment.label: Relative group size

definition.value: Relative group size: a time-varying variable capturing the number of individuals of the person's national origin (first- or second-generation immigrants) per thousand of the population aged 18-40 in the person's province of residence (one of 11 Danish NUTS-3 provinces). Measured on 1 January of year t and related to unions formed during the following year. Standardized in the model.

timing.value: Time-varying: measured on 1 January of each person-year t in the individual's province of residence, and related to unions formed during the following year.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from a different country of origin than the respondent's own. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized variable

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the standardized measure Relative group size is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, a one standard deviation increase in sex ratio decreases the odds of forming a first intraethnic union with a same-country immigrant, net of the cultural factors, the other opportunity structures and individual controls.

treatment.label: Sex ratio

definition.value: Within-group sex ratio: the proportion of men aged 18-40 divided by the proportion of women aged 18-40 in the national origin group in the province of residence, multiplied by 100; a value above 100 means more men than women in the group in the local partner market. timing.value: Time-varying: measured on 1 January of each person-year t in the individual's province of residence, and related to unions formed during the following year.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with an immigrant or second-generation immigrant from the same country of origin as the respondent. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized variable

magnitude.interpretation: a 14-percent decrease in the odds of intraethnic union formation

estimand.target_population: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 316792 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin

population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. claims.statement: Among male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, a one standard deviation increase in educational similarity is not significantly related to the odds of forming a first interethnic union with a native, net of the cultural factors, the other opportunity structures and individual controls.

treatment.label: Educational similarity

definition.value: Within-group educational similarity: the percentage of all opposite-sex members aged 25-40 of the national origin group in the province of residence who have the same educational level as the individual, using three educational levels (no vocational/professional qualification; vocational or short-cycle tertiary; medium- or long-cycle tertiary). Measured on 1 January of year t. Standardized in the model.

timing.value: Time-varying: measured on 1 January of each person-year t in the individual's province of residence, and related to unions formed during the following year.

definition.value: Event-specific discrete-time hazard of forming a first union with a native, i.e. a partner who and whose parents were born in Denmark. A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union; cohabiting unions are two persons at the same address with a common child, or two persons of different sexes whose age difference is below 15 years who share an address without being related by kinship. Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized variable

estimand.target_population: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Male 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 316792 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the standardized measure Educational similarity is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

A union is a legal marriage or a cohabiting union (see the paper's cohabitation definition). Coded as a binary person-year indicator and modelled against the reference category 'no event of that specific type'.

timing.value: Measured in annual person-years from age 18 (entry into the risk set, conditional on not already being in a union) until the first union formation or right censoring at death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period.

units.value: odds ratio per one standard deviation increase in the standardized variable

magnitude.interpretation: a 14-percent increase in the odds of intraethnic union formation

estimand.target_population: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark from 120 national origin groups, born 1966–1986, who were single at age 18 and are observed from age 18 until first union formation or censoring in the 1986–2016 period
estimand.time_horizon: Person-years of exposure from age 18 until first union formation, death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the observation period in 2016 — i.e. up to 22 years of exposure, averaged over the exposure window with time and time squared controlled.

population.description: Female 1.5- and second-generation immigrants in Denmark. 1.5-generation: born 1966–1986, aged 0–17 on arrival, resident in Denmark at age 18. Second generation: born in Denmark 1966–1986 to parents who were neither Danish citizens nor born in Denmark. 120 national origin groups; 219086 person-years in this model.
subgroups_defined: Western vs non-Western countries of origin
dominant religion of country of origin (Protestant, Catholic, other Christian, Muslim, Hindu/Buddhist/other)
language group of country of origin (Scandinavian, core Anglosphere, other English-speaking, other)
population.selection: Individuals enter the risk set on turning 18 only if they are not already in a union, and are followed until their first union formation or right censoring (death, emigration, age 40, or the end of the 1986–2016 observation period). Estimates are therefore conditional on being single at 18 and on remaining in Denmark and uncensored.

identification.source_of_variation: Between-country-of-origin variation across 120 national origin groups in dominant religion, Inglehart–Welzel value distance from Denmark and language group, plus year-to-year variation in opportunity structures (relative group size, within-group sex ratio, within-group educational similarity) within the 11 Danish provinces. No reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used; identification rests on conditioning on the observed covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Right censoring (death, emigration, reaching age 40, end of the observation period) is independent and noninformative: the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered. In the discussion the authors concede that some immigrants may have moved abroad to marry someone from their origin country, and argue this would make them underestimate the religion–intramarriage relationship.

formal.as_written: Under the assumptions of independent and noninformative censoring (i.e., the censoring mechanism does not depend on the time of the events or their distributions)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates in the model — the other cultural factors, the opportunity structures in the local partner market, time and time squared, generational status, educational attainment, start year, province and the national-origin-group random intercept — the standardized measure Educational similarity is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of union formation (no remaining confounding).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that disproportional growth in group size may confound the religion–union formation relationship and control for it; they report in Table A4 that religion coefficients are more pronounced when opportunity structures are omitted. No balance test or sensitivity analysis is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dominant religion, aggregate value scores and language of the country of origin validly proxy the cultural orientation of the individual immigrant and of his or her family and co-ethnic community.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No validation. The authors state the measures are imperfect because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations, and that personal religion is not observable in administrative registers.

key_assumptions.assumption: The multilevel discrete-time logit is correctly specified: the baseline logit hazard is quadratic in t, covariate effects enter additively and linearly on the log-odds scale, and the national-origin-group intercepts are draws from a common distribution.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The quadratic baseline is motivated by the inverse-U age pattern of union formation; the specification is not formally tested. Table A6 reports a multinomial logit alternative.

threats_discussed: Disproportional growth of non-Western and predominantly Muslim immigrant groups may confound the relationship between religion and union formation patterns.
Country-level religion, values and language misclassify individuals, because immigrants are selected subsamples of their origin populations and personal religion is not in the registers.
Right censoring may be informative if some immigrants move abroad to marry someone from their origin country.
Roommates of different sexes sharing an address may be misclassified as a cohabiting union.
Education is missing for approximately 20 percent of the analysis sample (handled with a missing category).
Value indexes are unavailable for about 25 percent of countries and are extrapolated from a neighbouring country.
Value measures are time-invariant, leaving time-varying country-level religion-related values unaddressed.
Perceived social status of immigrant groups among natives in the local partner market is not measured.
robustness_checks: Rerun excluding 1.5-generation immigrants, i.e. second generation only (Table A2, online supplement).
Rerun on immigrants from Muslim countries only (Table A3, online supplement).
Rerun controlling only for time-varying individual factors and not for opportunity structures (Table A4, online supplement).
Rerun only for those who turned 18 after 2002, to assess the 2002 '24-year rule' (Table A5, online supplement).
Replication with a multinomial logistic regression instead of the multivariate binary response approach (Table A6, online supplement).
unresolved_confounders: Personal religion and religiosity, which are not available in administrative registers.
Time-varying country-level religion-related values (the value measures are time-invariant).
Differences in the perceived social status of different immigrant groups among natives in the local partner markets.
Possible informative right censoring through marriage migration abroad.

ambiguities: The paper frames every estimate as an association ('relates to', 'predictor', 'associated with') rather than as a causal effect, while simultaneously arguing that it controls for confounding; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables on that basis.
The printed estimating equation carries α(r)1 on both t and t2, apparently a typographical error for α(r)2.
baseline_mean is not printed by the paper; the value recorded is the whole-sample mean person-year hazard derived from Table 3 and Table 4.

evidence.how: Table 3 (p. 488) reports 13271 union formations of this type for women; Table 4 (p. 490–491) reports 219086 person-years of exposure for women. The unconditional mean of the binary person-year outcome is 13271/219086 = 0.060574. The paper prints no reference-group (Protestant-country) mean, so this is the whole-sample mean hazard, not a control-group mean.
